facts.text: This paper is part of a series published by the National Governors Association (NGA) to identify actions Governors can take to guide their states and territories through intentional and effective power sector transformations.
For more information, please email fforrester@nga.org and dlauf@nga.org .
By taking advantage of these opportunities, Governors can build their state’s economy and create jobs that support grid modernization.
This has led to the commercial deployment of cost-effective and advanced grid technologies.
As generation facilities and the grid continue to age, threats to the grid become more prevalent, and increased demand exacerbates transmission carrying capacities.

It is important to recognize the benefits, costs, risks and other factors associated with the adoption of grid technologies and how their deployment would impact the broader energy system and energy consumers.

With these transformative trends in process, Governors are eager to support deployment of technology solutions to facilitate their policy objectives and meet increased loads – and doing so while maintaining or even improving grid reliability, resilience and affordability.

Similarly, high-tech innovations can often be paired with more traditional, low-tech and low-cost solutions to achieve optimal results, such as utility resilience programs that pair distribution automation with system hardening and vegetation management to improve reliability or grid-enhancing technology deployment considered alongside transmission expansion.
Grid modernizing technologies can help integrate DERs into the broader electrical grid and use the growing pool of DERs for grid services that strengthen the broader system.
These goals can establish a Governor’s broad energy policy vision and instigate policy actions that will lead to grid modernization.
Strengthening these structures and approaching grid modernization from a comprehensive planning perspective will create an environment for sustained innovation within the electrical sector.

In addition to increasing the role of states in transmission planning and cost allocation, Order 1920 includes a requirement for transmission providers to consider alternative transmission technologies, including dynamic line ratings, advanced power flow controllers, and advanced conductors.
Department of Energy award , this project will deploy dynamic line rating technology and other grid improvements across 1,125 miles of existing transmission lines.
That’s the opportunity behind advanced transmission technology being deployed across Arkansas, Louisiana and Mississippi — and one of the most innovative parts of the project arrives by drone.

“DLR gives us real-time insight into how much electricity a line can safely carry under actual weather conditions, helping us move more energy across the grid using existing infrastructure,” Sansing said.
Ultimately, the goal is to use innovation to make better use of infrastructure already in place, strengthen the grid and support the communities and industries that depend on reliable electricity.
Pictured: Jonathan McGinnis, project manager for Heimdall Power; Ann Charlotte Valheim, chief deployment officer, Heimdall Power; and Tim Sansing, senior engineer, Entergy.
Katie Jereza, assistant secretary for the U.S.
Career opportunities Entergy surveys in progress

Increasing capacity on existing lines could help defer some future transmission investments, which can take years to plan and build, while providing operators with more information to manage changing conditions across the system.
